S.K. Sinha for B.N. Chowdhury ------ For the petitioner in all the three Rules. 
M. Shehabulla with Syed Mahmud Hossain  ------ For Opp. Party No. 1 in all the three Rules.
parties:
Haladhar Dutta ------Petitioner

case_source: (In the meter of an application under section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for setting aside the order date 27.12.1980 passed by Sub-Judge, Noakhali in Misc. Appeal No 122, 121, 123 of 1978 affirming those of Munsif, 2nd Court, Feni in Misc. Case Nos. 129, 128 and 139 of 1972 passed on 30.6.78 )
full_judgment:
These three Rules have been obtained by the pre-emptor-petitioner calling in question the judgment and order dated 27.12.80 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali in Miscellaneous Appeals No. 121, 122 and 125 of 1978 affirming the judgment and order dated 30.6.78 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Feni in Miscellaneous Cases No. 128, 129 and 139 of 1972 rejecting the prayer for pre-emption, made under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Since all the Rules have arisen out of the same judgment, the same have been heard analogously and this judgment shall govern all the cases.

2. The common case of the petitioner in all the three miscellaneous cases is that he is the co-sharer by inheritance in C.S. Khatian No. 803 of mouza Chandpur and lands recorded therein originally belonged to Shafi Kumar, Kali Kumar, Krishna Chandra, RajKumar, Nakshatra and Sharoda and that he is the son of Krishna Chandra and that opposite party No. 2 is also a co-sharer by inheritance in the aforesaid C.S. Khatian No. 803, that the opposite party No. 2 by three different kabalas sold some portion of the disputed plot to the opposite party No. 1 in the year 1972 and .did not serve any notice of such transfer to him and that the opposite party No. 1 is a stranger-purchaser, that he is in possession of some portion of the disputed plot in his maliki right. Thus he is entitled to pre-empt the disputed lands.

3.  The pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 contested the cases by filling written objection and alleging, inter alia, that the petitioner was not a co-sharer in respect of the disputed property with regard to which two khatians under S.A. operation, namely Khatian Nos. 844 and 845 have been prepared and the disputed land has been recorded in new Khatian No. 845 and that the land recorded in Khatian No. 844 belonged to the petitioner. Thus after splitting up of the original khatian i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 803 the petitioner is not entitled to claim himself as a co-sharer. tenant in the disputed khatian No. 845. The further cases of the opposite party No. 1 is that the land in dispute is a debuttor property and as such the petitioner is not entitled to claim any pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the pre-emption petitions upon holding that the vendors of opposite party No. 1, namely Phani and Khogendra, are the tenants in the separately recorded M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 845 at jama of Tk. 7/14 annas and the M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 844 stands recorded in the name of the petitioner along with his other co-sharers. Thus the interest of the vendors of the opposite party No. 1 in their parent C.S. Khatiaa No. 803 was no longer in existence while the impugned transfer took place. The learned Munsif also declined to consider whether the parent Khatian No. 803 was legally spitted up into two khatians, namely, M.R.O.R. Khatian Nos. 844 and 845. Thus the learned Munsif  held that the petitioner has no locus standi to claim pre-emption in respect of the disputed land.

5. Against the judgment and order of the trial Court the petitioner preferred the above mentioned miscellaneous appeals and the lower appellate Court by the impugned judgment and order dismissed the appeals and affirmed the judgment of the trial Court upon taking the same view that the parent khatian i.e C.S. Khatian No. 805 having been separated into two khatians and the disputed land having been recorded in the new khatian No. 845, the petitioner is not a co-sharer in respect of the disputed land.

6. Mr. S.K. Sinha, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has raised two points for all the three Rules. Firstly, that the opening of two separate jamas under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by way of sub-division of the original jama i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 801 having not been done in accordance with law, the Courts below committed an error of law in holding that on the basis of two separate khatians the pre-emptor, although is admittedly a son of the original owner, lost his right of claim to be a co-sharer in respect of the disputed property. Secondly, that the petitioner also claimed that he is the contiguous owner of the disputed land but the Courts below failed to consider his case as to whether he could prove his claim as the contiguous owner of the disputed land.

7. Mr.M. Shehabullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 contends that the parent jama was separated at the instance of the pre-emptor as well as his other co-sharers and on the basis of separate khatians, namely, Khatian Nos. 844 and 845 they have been paying rents in respect of the disputed land. Thus the Courts below legally held that the pre-emptor lost his right of claiming pre-emption as a co-sharer. The learned Advocate further submits that the pre-emptor in his petition for pre-emption did not specifically plead that he is also a contiguous owner of the disputed land and nothing also transpires from the judgments of the Courts below that the pre-emptor also pressed his claim that he is entitled to pre-empt the land as contiguous owner. The learned Advocate in his affidavit-in-opposition has annexed true copy of the petition of miscellaneous case No. 128 of 1972 and in paragraph 8 of the said-affidavit it is stated that the petitioner did not claim his right of pre-emption as a contiguous owner too.

8. At the time of issuance of the Rules records were not called for. But on being asked the learned Advocate for the petitioner produced the certified copy of the depositions of the witnesses. Since nothing has been mentioned in the judgments of the Courts below regarding the oral evidence of the parties, for my personal satisfaction have perused the evidence of the witnesses of both The sides from the certified copies of the depositions. It is evident from the Annexure-1 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner has stated that he along with the vendor of the opposite party No. 1 is co-sharer by inheritance in C.S. Khatian No. 803 and that he is in possession in some portion of the disputed plot in his maliki right. In the Schedule be has mentioned the original Khatian No. 803 as well as the present Khatian No. 845. The disputed plots are Plots No. 846 and 850 measuring the total area of 1.84 and, 69 decimals respectively.

<u>9. Admittedly, two separate khatians under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have been prepared in respect of the land of the original jama i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 803. The Courts below have observed that these two khatians are the modified record-of-right Nothing transpires either from the evidence 91 the parties or from the judgments of the Courts below that those khatians have been-finally published and accepted under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as final. There are two provisions under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act regarding preparation of the record-of-rights. Under section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in view of the notification of the Government under section 17 of the Act a draft record-of-right was prepared for the purpose of acquisition of the rent-receiving interest or under the same provisions the record of right that was prepared under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act would have been revised in respect of any district, part of a district or of any local area as the Government would deem fit and necessary; The particulars which are required to be incorporated under those draft record-of-rights have been mentioned in the rules framed for the purpose. A judicial notice can be taken that the draft or the revised khatians that were directed to be prepared under section 19 of the Act was not finally published since before coming into force of Part V or the Act, which came into operation in the Noakhali district on 1.8.63. After coming into force of whole of the Part V a radical change in the scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was brought in, whereby in view of sub-section (8) of section 82 the words 'raiyati' or 'tenant' as well as 'rent' were to be deemed to have been substituted by the words 'milk' an 'land revenue'. Chapter V of the Act also brought in the incident of tenancy including the right of occupancy as well as devolution of interest by way of inheritance. In view of sections . 83 and 84 of the Act. Thus question of status of the malik as well as the co-sharer malik, as are to be read in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in view of the, provisions of section- 82 (8) of the Act, gave a new dimension in the rights and liabilities including the right to pre-empt by a co-sharer malik in respect of the transfer of any holding or portion thereof by a ma to any stranger. Section 96 has also brought a new right of pre-emption for the owners of the contiguous lands. Under section 19 provisions have been made only to prepare a draft record-of-right or to revise the re-cord-of-right prepared and finally published under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act. After coming into force of Part-V and giving the raiyats of different natures to a single status of malik, the right to hold or occupy such land for agricultural or horticultural purposes on payment of revenue direct to the Government. The word 'tenant' as has been defined under section 2(27) of the Act lost is connotation as was initially defined. It is evident that in Part—V provision has been made under section 117 of the Act for amalgamation, consolidation or subdivision of holdings. In .case of amalgamation or consolidation of holdings under section 117 (1) (a), (b) the revenue officer either of his own motion or upon any application made to him in that behalf is entitled to amalgamate or consolidate the holdings. But so far the sub-division of holdings is concerned under section 117(1) (c) of the Act it has been made imperative that the sub-division of joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof can be made by the revenue officer only upon an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants and no order for such sub-division shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and to be heard by him in the matter. It has further been provided under sub-section (3) of section 117 that that when an order under sub section (1) has been passed sub-dividing a joint holding, such sub-division may be demarcated on the ground and shown on the cadastral survey map. Thus the scheme of sub-division is very much clear for the purpose of adjudication that has been provided under Chapter XII of Part-V of the Act.</u>

<u>10. The modified record-of-right, as in evident from the provision of sec. 46 of the Act, was required to be prepared and considered for the purpose of final publication of the compensation assessment roll regarding acquisition of all kind of rent receiving interest under the Act. The record of right derives its presumptive value of correctness both under section 19 of the Act as well as section 144 of the Act. In the absence of any final publication of the record of right which have been prepared under the Act either under section 19 or under section 144, there cannot be any presumptive value of its correctness which is required to be rebutted. It does not a from the judgments of the Courts below that they considered as to whether this sub-division of the original jama was done upon the application of the pre-emptor or with notice to him as provided under section 117 (1) (c) of the Act. Preparation of the record-of-right under Chapter IV was for the purpose of acquisition of rent receiving interest whereas the purpose of preparation of the record-of right under Part-V, Chapter-XIV is for maintaining the proper and up-to-date settlement rent roll. It should be significantly noted that whenever the raiyat or under raiyat or any other raiyat as they had been under the Bengal Tenancy Act, alter coming into force of Part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 have been merged into a single status of malik having their equal rights and liabilities including the right to pre-empt any land under section 96 of the Act. Thus in the absence of any material or evidence on record that such separation of original jama was done in accordance with section 117(1) (c) of is not at all safe to oust a co-sharer malik from exercising his vested right only on the basis of two M.R.O R. Khatians which were prepared initially for the purpose of realisation of rent pending final publication of record-of-right as has been contemplated under the scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>11. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the opposite party that on the basis of two new khatians the vendors of the opposite party as well as the pre-emptor have been paying rent separately but it does not appear from the judgments of the Courts below that they had the opportunity of considering any materials regarding such payment of rent which would give some light as to the point of time since when they started paying rent. The Courts below have proceeded on the footing that so far the exercising of the right of pre-emption is concerned under section 96 of the Act on the basis of the claim of co-shareship in the holding, mere showing the payment of land revenue under two different numbers in the tenants ledger is sufficient to give a complete negation to any vested right of pre-emption. There cannot be doubt, of course, whenever all the co-sharers of the original C.S. Khatian amicably, split up the jama for the purpose of facilitating payment of land revenue that can be construed as very much identical to the amicable partition amongst such co-sharers. In such a case by their conduct amongst them-selves the co-sharers would dis-entitle them-selves from claiming any benefit of a joint tenancy in view of the doctrine of estoppel, as has been provided under section 115 of the Evidence Act. "</u>

<u>12. Thus in resolving the dispute in the instant case, in my opinion, it is necessary to look into the legality of the sub-division of the original holding in the light of the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. since in a application for pre-emption the Court of law is under the legal obligation to decide-certain basic rights of the parties.</u>

<u>Moreover, the pre-emptor in the application for pre-emption has asserted that he is in possession in a portion of the disputed plots in his maliki right and two of his witnesses, namely, P.Ws. 2 and 3 have deposed that the pre-emptor has the land contiguous to the disputed plots. Thus it was also the duty of the Court below to consider as to whether the pre-emptor is a contiguous owner of the disputed plots, since it is not the case of either of the party that such sub-division was finally effected under section 117(3) of the Act. I do not find any light from the judgments of the Courts below as to whether the land of the plots under pre-emption has also been recorded in the other M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 844. In support of the contention, Mr. M. Shebabullah. the learned Advocate has referred to a decision reported in 29 DLR. 153 in which the original C.S. Khatian was split up into four different khatians and in respect of such split up khatians pre-emption was sought for by the owner of the other khatians, where it has been decided that since those khatians were amicably allowed to be prepared out of the parent khatian, the pre-emptor and his other co. sharers virtually waived their right to claim co-sharership into the disputed khatians. Since I do not find any material that in the instant case the two khatians were allowed to be prepared amicably by the co-sharers, in my opinion, the decision reported in 29 D.L R. is distinguishable on facts. Mr. S.K. Sinha, learned Advocate in support of his contention has also cited a decision reported in 33 D.L.R. (A. D.) 323 in the case of Md. A. Rouf and others vs. Mahmuda Khatun and others. He has also referred to another case reported in the same volume of 33 D.L.R. (A.D.) 309. from the decision reported in 3 D.L.R (A. D.) it is clear, so far as the sub-division of the original holding is concerned under section I l7(1)-c) of the Act, that it is mandatory to notify all other co-sharers before passing order for such subdivision. In the instant case since no material is available from the judgments of the Courts below that such sub-division of holding was done either amicably or by an application under section 117(1)(c) of the Act, I am afraid to come to any definite conclusion that the pre-emptor has either lost his right of pre-emption as a co-sharer or his interest in the original jamal still exists. In such view of the matter I am of the opinion that for the interest of justice the applications for pre-emption should be heard by the trial court afresh.</u>

13. For the reasons as started above, I find substance in these Rules and, accordingly, I make these Rules absolute and set aside the judgments and orders of the Courts below and send back the miscellaneous cases to the trial court on remand for rehearing on the basis of materials on record and allow the parties of opportunity to adduce further evidence for the purpose of the Court to adjudicate upon the dispute effectively and completely between the parties.

In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

End.
